title: Sad and Happy at the Same Time

pages.text:
Saturday seventy-four, 10:30 a.m. The garage door slammed shut, and the sharp, angry rhythm of drumsticks started beating against the metal.

On the first Saturday, I would have run to the front door. I would have shouted, then I would have lost. But this time, I walked straight to the garage. I didn't knock. I just leaned against the doorframe with my arms crossed and waited for the tapping to stop. It didn't.

"Max," Tessa said without looking up. Her back was to me, and her sticks were tapping a furious beat on the side of the washing machine. "This is my practice pad. And my posters. And my band."

"You're right," I said. "It is."

She spun around. Her purple streak was wild, and her eyes were wet. "What are you doing here? Do you want to fight? Because I have sticks and you have a hoodie."

"I'm sorry about your band," I said.

The tapping stopped. The silence was loud.

"I don't know what you're talking about," she said, but her voice shook.

"The Kettle Drums," I said. "You're scared you're going to lose them. I'm sad about it too. I'm not going to play for the Dunmore Rockets again, either."

I didn't wait for her to react. I sat down on the concrete floor, back against the wall. She stared at me for a long time, then sat down next to me, leaving a very precise foot of space between us.

We didn't speak for five minutes.

"You're weird today," she finally said.

"Thanks," I said.
pages.image: Two siblings sit on a concrete garage floor, backs against a metal door; a boy in a red hoodie and a girl with a purple hair streak sit side by side, looking at the floor, with drumsticks resting on a washing machine behind them.

pages.text:
Saturday seventy-five, 11:00 a.m.

I sat on the kitchen steps eating a cracker when I spotted the helmet through the window. It was blue with a scratch on the visor. Jonah stood on the porch, waving his hand.

I looked down at the cracker. I looked up at the helmet.

Something in my chest felt like it was trying to escape through my ears. I wasn't sad because the day was bad. I was sad because it was good. Jonah was here. He was real. He was probably going to be in Tucson with me, or maybe he wasn't, and either way, saying goodbye to this porch was going to hurt.

My eyes burned. I refused to blink. I chewed the cracker until it turned to dust.

I stood up, wiped my face with my sleeve, and walked to the door.

On the first Saturday, I had ignored the bell. I had hidden on the roof. I had let him call my name until it sounded like a stranger's.

I opened the door.

"Hey," I said.

Jonah grinned, his whole face lighting up. "I have a plan."

"I know," I said. "I'm coming."

He blinked. Then he grinned wider.

Sadness and joy, I thought. They weren't fighting. They were riding in the same car.
pages.image: A boy in a red hoodie stands in a doorway opening a screen door, looking at a tall boy with a buzz cut wearing a blue bike helmet who is smiling widely on a porch; morning light, a yellow house exterior.

pages.text:
Saturday seventy-six.

I decided to test a new rule: pick one good thing per hour and say it out loud. At 9:15, the box marked FRAGILE dropped. Mom dove for it, sliding sideways across the tile like a hockey puck on ice. She caught it with one hand and landed hard on her hip, looking stunned.

"Nice dive, Mom," I said.

She blinked, surprised. "Thanks, Max."

At 12:30, we ate peanut butter sandwiches on paper towels because the table was a box. The paper was crisp, which made the sandwich taste better, like biting into a cracker instead of a sad slice of bread.

"This is actually good," I said.

Dad looked up from his own sandwich, his mustache twitching. "Really?"

"Yeah. It's like a taco, but with bread."

Dad laughed, a full, round sound that bounced off the bare walls.

At 2:00, Jonah was waiting on the porch. I was wearing my big grey sneakers, the ones with the double knots.

"Shoes you can get wet," I said.

"Correct," Jonah said.

I put them on. They were tight, squeezing my toes, but I was ready. I picked the wet shoes.
pages.image: A boy in a red hoodie sits on a kitchen floor eating a sandwich on paper, while a man in a fish apron looks up from his own food; cardboard boxes are stacked in the background, the scene is warm and casual.

pages.text:
Saturday seventy-seven.

I let the day be bad.

It started raining at four o'clock, which is wrong because Saturdays in Dunmore are usually bright and loud. The rain fell thick and gray, drenching Mr. Grady's sprinkler as it sprayed blindly into the storm. The mailman stood under the awning, dripping like a drowned squirrel, and he was laughing. Not smiling. Laughing.

I climbed to the roof. I sat on the wet shingles, my red hoodie dark with water, and watched the gutters overflow. The cold seeped into my bones, making me feel as heavy as the wet leaves piling up in the yard. I stayed there for an hour, just watching the water run.

Then I went inside, soaked and shivering. Dad was making pizza. The smell of pepperoni hit me, thick and warm, cutting through the damp air of the house.

"I'm sad," I said to the air, to Dad, to the dough. "And I'm going to have pizza anyway."

He handed me a slice without saying a word.

I ate it on the floor. It didn't taste like sadness. It tasted like dinner.
pages.image: A boy in a red hoodie sits on the floor of a living room, holding a slice of pizza, while a man in a fish apron stands behind a counter; rain is visible through a window, the interior is dim and warm with lamplight.

pages.text:
I went to my room and found the closet door standing open, revealing the inside panel where my history lived.

Seventy-seven pencil scratches. I had made them myself, one by one, over what felt like a lifetime.

I stared at the jagged lines for a long time. For seventy-six Saturdays, I had been convinced that choosing to be happy was just a fancy word for pretending I wasn't sad. I thought I had to pick a side, like a binary code, happy or sad, one or the other, and that mixing them would make me crazy.

I was wrong.

Everyone in my house had been doing that for weeks, too. Dad was pretending the toast wasn't burnt. Mom was pretending the checklist was enough. Tessa was pretending she wasn't scared of the new school. I was pretending I didn't care. But pretending is a heavy coat to wear all day. It doesn't mean you don't feel the bad thing; it means you decide what's going to drive.

I looked at the door, then down the hallway where the clock stood silent. I picked up my pencil. I didn't add a mark. I just held it. I was ready to try the hardest apology of my life.
